name: Shibuya Crossing
label: Shibuya Crossing
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/291758776: the OpenStreetMap point 'Shibuya Scramble Crossing'.

text.description:
Shibuya Crossing is the big pedestrian junction outside Shibuya Station, and it is one of the most recognisable street scenes in Tokyo. When the lights turn red for the cars, people cross in every direction at once. The Wikipedia figures put it at roughly 1,000 to 2,000 people on a single green light, and it has been called the world's busiest pedestrian crossing. It opened in 1973 and has appeared in many films, TV shows and music videos, so many visitors already know the view before they arrive.

It photographs well because of the movement and the scale. Crowds, tall buildings and video screens all fit into one frame, and the scene changes with every light cycle. You can take a wide shot of the whole junction or a tighter picture of a few people crossing. The same spot works as a short video clip too.

Standing there gives you a longer view, and the telephoto lens helps you pick out a section of the crowd. Wait for a new green light, because the crowd fills up in the first few seconds. Keep to the pavement and the crossing islands, and do not stop in the road to take a picture. Hold your phone firmly in a busy crowd. Around Halloween and New Year's Eve the area gets very crowded and the local ward has put restrictions in place, so expect rules and tighter security then. Right next to it: Hachikō statue.
text.geographic_location: Shibuya Crossing is in the Shibuya district of central Tokyo, right outside Shibuya Station, with the crossing lying to the north-west of the station. It sits in a major shopping and entertainment area.
text.directions_text: Start at Shibuya station, which is served by the JR Saikyo Line, JR Shonan-Shinjuku Line, JR Yamanote Line, Tokyo Metro - Denentoshi bypass line, Tokyo Metro Fukutoshin Line, Tokyo Metro Ginza Line and Tokyo Metro Hanzōmon Line. The crossing is about 174 m to the north-west of the station, about 3 minutes on foot. If you prefer a quieter approach, Meiji-jingumae 'Harajuku' station (Tokyo Metro Chiyoda Line and Tokyo Metro Fukutoshin Line) is about 1,095 m north of the crossing. The phone icon on the map is about 50 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole junction. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) from where you stand to bring the crowd and buildings closer. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are close to the crossing and want to include the tall buildings and screens.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 50 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. From there you view the junction from a distance, so use zoom rather than walking closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the verticals of the buildings straight. Put the crowd on the lower third of the frame and leave room above for the buildings and screens. Take a few shots as each light cycle starts, when the crowd is at its fullest. Try a short Live Photo to catch the flow of people.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the crowd to set focus, then use the exposure slider to bring the brightness down a little so bright screens don't wash out. In the evening, night mode helps, but hold the phone very still because people are moving. Do not use portrait mode on a distant scene.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into the evening usually works well, when the video screens and shop lights stand out against the darker sky. Weekday daytimes are often less packed than evenings and weekends. Avoid Halloween and New Year's Eve unless you want the biggest crowds.

text.access_note: The crossing is an open public road junction that you can use freely on foot; if you want an elevated view from a building, check the official site before you go.

text.description:
Tokyo Skytree is a broadcasting and observation tower in Sumida, and at 634 m it is the tallest tower in Japan. It reached that height in early 2011 and opened to the public on 22 May 2012. The number is a word game: 6, 3 and 4 can be read as "Musashi", an old name for the region. The lattice is painted a bluish-white shade called "Skytree White", based on a traditional Japanese colour. The base is a three-legged structure, which gives the tower a distinctive shape from the street.

It photographs well because it is so tall and so clean in outline, with plain sky behind it on a clear day. At night the LED lighting alternates daily between a sky-blue pattern and a purple one, so the tower can look quite different from one evening to the next.

Tall subjects are easiest when you keep the phone upright and level. Tilting it upwards makes the tower lean inwards. Step back to the edge of the open space if you can, and include some foreground, such as a lamp post or a passer-by, to give a sense of height. The observation decks are a separate matter, so check the official site before you go if you plan to go up.
text.geographic_location: Tokyo Skytree stands in Sumida, in the east of Tokyo, about seven km north-east of Tokyo Station. The nearest stations are Oshiage (Toei Asakusa Line) and Oshiage (SKYTREE) (Tokyo Metro Hanzōmon Line), both a short walk to the east of the tower. It is the centerpiece of a large commercial development owned by Tobu Railway.

Oshiage (SKYTREE) (Tokyo Metro Hanzōmon Line) is about 4 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 220 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole tower from this close. The default lens (1x) works for the upper part or a tighter, simpler shot. A telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is good for the top section against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 220 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. The tower will be straight ahead of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on your gridlines and line up the tower with a vertical line to keep it from leaning. Hold the phone upright and level, then raise your arms rather than tilting the phone back. Leave some sky above the tip and add a little foreground at the bottom for scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so the white lattice does not wash out against bright sky. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a railing or your body so the lights stay sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, when the sun is behind you in the east and lights the side of the tower facing you. Dusk and after dark are good for the illumination, which alternates daily between sky blue and purple.

text.access_note: The tower can be photographed from the surrounding public streets, but the observation decks are a ticketed visit, so check the official site before you go.

text.description:
Tokyo Tower is a steel lattice tower in Minato, finished in 1958 and clearly modelled on the Eiffel Tower. It stands 332.9 metres tall and is painted white and international orange, which is a requirement for air safety. For more than fifty years it was the tallest tower in Japan, until Tokyo Skytree overtook it in 2012. It still works as a broadcast mast, and visitors can go up to two observation decks, at 150 m and about 250 m. The tower is repainted on a regular cycle, so its colours tend to look fresh.

It photographs well because the criss-cross frame and bold colours make strong patterns, and the shape is instantly recognisable. The phone icon on the map is about 40 m north-east of the subject. Here the tower becomes a towering, graphic shape rather than a distant landmark. Looking up through the legs and cross-bracing gives a dramatic, slightly abstract picture that suits a phone well.

You will not fit the whole tower in at this distance without the ultra-wide lens, so decide whether you want the full height or a close-up of the structure. Take a few of each. Keep your phone clean, as the sky behind the tower is bright and any smudge will show. If the area is busy, wait a moment for people to move out of the foreground, or include them to give a sense of scale.
text.geographic_location: Tokyo Tower is in the Shiba-koen district of Minato, Tokyo.

Use the default lens (1x) for the lower section and the cross-bracing. If your phone has a telephoto lens (2x-5x), use it for close-ups of the lattice pattern and the orange and white paintwork.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 40 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. Take a few steps to either side to change how the legs and beams line up.

Line the central axis up with a vertical gridline for a symmetrical shot. For something more abstract, fill the frame with the lattice at 2x or more, or place the tower off-centre with plenty of sky around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the tower's orange to focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly so the bright sky does not wash out the paintwork. In the evening, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime gives the clearest view of the white and orange paintwork, especially under a blue sky. After dark the tower is usually lit, which suits night mode, but check the lighting yourself on the day.

label: Akihabara

text.description:
Akihabara is Tokyo's "Electric Town", a busy shopping district in Chiyoda ward built around Akihabara Station. It is known for video games, anime, manga and electronics, and for the colourful character artwork that covers many shopfronts. Cosplayers hand out flyers on the pavements, mostly for maid cafés, and there are large arcades along the streets. That mix of signs, screens and people is what makes it fun to photograph with a phone.

The name comes from Akibagahara. After a fire in 1869 destroyed the area, a shrine to a fire-controlling deity was built there, and the locals nicknamed it Akiba. The Electric Town label came after the Second World War, when the area was a black market and then a centre for household electrical goods. From the 1980s the shops shifted towards computers, and later anime, manga and games.

For photos, think in layers: the tall signs above, the shopfronts at street level and the people in between. Look for frames that include a few signs at different depths rather than one flat wall. Keep your phone at chest height and watch for passers-by, as the pavements are busy. If you want to photograph someone in costume, ask first. Check before shooting inside shops.
text.geographic_location: Akihabara sits in Tokyo's Chiyoda ward, in the streets around Akihabara Station, mostly just west of the station. Part of the district falls in the Sotokanda and Kanda-Sakumachō areas.
text.directions_text: The nearest station is Akihabara (JR Chuo-Sobu Line, JR Keihin-Tohoku-Negishi Line, JR Yamanote Line and Tokyo Metro Hibiya Line). The subject area lies to the west of it, about 1 minute on foot (about 54 m). Iwamotocho (Toei Shinjuku Line) is also close: the subject area is to its north-west, about 6 minutes on foot (about 372 m). Start at the phone icon on the map and walk south, about 5 minutes on foot, following the main shopping street on the west side of the station. The phone icon on the map is about 170 m north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for street scenes that look natural. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) when you want tall signs and shopfronts in one frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as a single sign or a figure on a shopfront.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 170 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up vertical signs with the grid so buildings don't lean. Hold the phone level and include a foreground such as a pavement or crossing for depth. For a busier shot, wait a moment for people to pass through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest sign to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the colours don't blow out. If the light is low, try night mode and keep your arms tucked in to avoid blur. Live Photos can capture the movement of the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into the evening usually gives the best mix of daylight and lit signs. Weekday mornings are generally calmer if you want fewer people in the shot.

text.access_note: The streets are public and open to walk around, but individual shops, arcades and cafés have their own rules, so check before photographing inside.

text.description:
Shibuya Sky is the observation deck on the roof of Shibuya Scramble Square, a tall mixed-use tower built right over Shibuya Station. The tower is 229.71 m high and opened on 1 November 2019. It became the tallest building in the Shibuya district, so the view from the top is wide and open. The building is named after the famous Shibuya Scramble Crossing, which lies just a few metres away, so the busy crossing is part of the story of any picture you take here.

For a phone photographer the appeal is the height. You can look out over the station area and the surrounding city, with the crossing and its streams of people far below you. The phone icon on the map is at the building itself, so the shot is taken from up on the deck. Pick one clear subject for each photo, such as the crossing, a block of towers or the skyline, rather than trying to fit everything in.

Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view, then try the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the sweep of the city. The telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is good for picking out the crossing or a single building. Turn on gridlines to keep the horizon straight. If you are shooting through glass, press your lens close to it and tilt it slightly to cut reflections. Check the official site before you go for how to visit.
text.geographic_location: Shibuya Sky is on top of Shibuya Scramble Square, in the Shibuya district of Tokyo, about 30 m south of Shibuya Station and a few metres from the Shibuya Scramble Crossing.

The building is about 30 m to the south of the station, about 1 minute on foot. The building's lower floors connect directly to the station, so you can follow the signs inside. If you come out at street level, walk south and the tower is right there. Meiji-jingumae 'Harajuku' (Tokyo Metro Chiyoda Line and Tokyo Metro Fukutoshin Line) is a longer option: the building is about 1,170 m to the south of it, about 19 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on a top or bottom line. Choose one subject, such as the crossing far below or a row of towers, and let the rest of the city fill the background. Keep your lens close to any glass to avoid reflections.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the part of the city you want sharp, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the buildings keep their detail. After dark, try night mode and hold the phone steady against a rail or your body for a few seconds.

text.description: Sensō-ji is Tokyo's oldest established temple, dedicated to Kannon, the bodhisattva of compassion. It sits in the old entertainment district of Asakusa and draws more than 30 million visitors a year. Its pull for photographers is the sequence of scenes: the Kaminarimon, or Thunder Gate, with its huge red-and-black paper lantern; the shop-lined Nakamise-dōri; the Hōzōmon gate; and then the main hall and five-story pagoda. Shops have stood along the approach since 1685, so the street still feels like a pilgrim's route, even though the buildings are newer. The temple was destroyed in the air raid of 10 March 1945. The main hall was rebuilt between 1951 and 1958 with a titanium-tiled roof that keeps the historic look. The Kaminarimon was rebuilt in 1960, the Hōzōmon in 1964 and the pagoda in 1973. The bold reds and the long, layered view down the approach suit a phone camera well, and the people passing through give the pictures a sense of scale. Expect crowds, so be patient and wait for small gaps rather than trying to clear the frame. Stay out of the flow of walkers when you stop to shoot.
text.geographic_location: Sensō-ji is in the Asakusa district of Tokyo, marked on the map at about 35.7147° N, 139.7968° E. Asakusa Shrine stands right next to it on the east side, and Nakamise-dōri leads up to the temple from the Kaminarimon gate.
text.directions_text: Start at Asakusa station, served by the Toei Asakusa Line and the Tokyo Metro Ginza Line. It is about 9 minutes on foot, with the temple to the north. Tawaramachi station on the Tokyo Metro Ginza Line is a little further, about 12 minutes on foot, with the temple to the north-east. The phone icon on the map is about 110 m south of the numbered pin. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the gate, the lantern and the long view of the approach. Switch to the default lens (1x) for the main hall and the Hōzōmon. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the roof, the pagoda and the lantern's painted pattern.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 110 m south of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. From there the temple lies to the north, straight ahead of you. Stay to the side of the walking path so you are not blocking other visitors.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the central path with a vertical grid line, so the buildings look straight. Let the crowd fill the foreground to give a sense of scale. Keep the red gate and roofs well inside the frame, and hold the phone level to avoid leaning verticals. For a detail shot, zoom in on one subject, such as a roof corner or lantern, rather than the whole scene.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a mid-tone part of the building to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the reds stay rich and the sky does not wash out. If you are shooting after dark, use night mode and brace your arms against your body to keep the phone steady. Try a Live Photo to catch a clean moment between passers-by.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the morning is usually calmer, and you will find it easier to get a clear view. Late afternoon and evening can add warm light or lit-up buildings, though the crowds may be larger.

text.access_note: Sensō-ji is an active Buddhist temple, so dress and behave respectfully, and check the official site before you go for any access rules.

text.description: Meiji Shrine is a Shinto shrine in Shibuya, dedicated to Emperor Meiji and his wife, Empress Shōken. It sits inside a forest of about 70 hectares, with roughly 120,000 trees of 365 species. All of them were donated from across Japan when the shrine was founded. That is why a photo here can feel calm and green even though you are in the middle of Tokyo. The shrine was built in the traditional nagare-zukuri style, using mainly Japanese cypress and copper. The original buildings were destroyed in the Second World War air raids, and the present shrine was finished in 1958 after a public fund-raising effort. For your phone, the appeal is the contrast between the warm wooden structures and the deep green trees around them. Start with a wide shot to show how the buildings sit among the trees. Then move closer for details such as the roofline and the timber. Take a few steps to one side to keep other visitors out of the frame, and wait a moment for gaps in the crowd. Keep your phone low-key and your voice down, as this is an active place of worship.
text.geographic_location: Meiji Shrine is in the Shibuya district of Tokyo, set in a large forest beside Yoyogi Park. Harajuku station (JR Yamanote Line) lies to its south-east, and Kita-sando station (Tokyo Metro Fukutoshin Line) is also close by.

Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for roof details and timber, and to pick out features further away.

shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the verticals straight, so that the trees and buildings do not lean. Include a bit of path or foreground to give depth. For a second shot, go in tighter on the roof and wood with the telephoto and let the green trees fill the background.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the building to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky or sunlit stone looks washed out. Under the trees the light can be patchy, so check the shot before you move on. Live Photos can catch people walking through the scene, but a still is usually better here.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soon after the gates open at sunrise is usually calmer and the light is gentle. Later in the day the light can be patchy under the trees, so check the exposure.

text.description: Golden Gai is a tight huddle of tiny bars in Shinjuku, made up of six narrow alleys joined by passageways barely wide enough for one person. More than 200 little bars, clubs and eateries are squeezed in, most of them in two-storey buildings only a few feet wide, with steep stairs up to a second bar or a small flat. It photographs well because it shows a side of Tokyo that has mostly been redeveloped away: wider roads and tall buildings now surround it. Up close you get crowded signs, posters plastered over ramshackle walls and dim, moody light. The area dates back to at least the 1960s for some of its bars, and it survived the 1980s, when many Tokyo buildings were set on fire so developers could buy the land, because supporters took turns guarding it at night. One important point before you lift your phone: the alleys are private roads, and the sources say that taking photographs or video on the street needs permission from the area's business promotion association. Please check the current rules and any signs on the spot, and respect them. Most bars don't open until about 9 or 10 pm, so the area is very quiet by day and in the early evening. Keep your phone low-key, avoid pointing it at customers or into doorways, and never block a narrow passage.

text.description:
Ueno Park is a big, green public park in the Ueno district of Taitō, and it works well as a relaxed photo walk rather than a single viewpoint. It opened in 1873 on land that had belonged to the temple of Kan'ei-ji, which makes it one of Japan's first public parks. Today it draws over ten million visitors a year. The phone icon on the map is a little way north of the park.

There is plenty to photograph. In spring the park is known for its cherry blossom, with some 800 cherry trees in the park itself. Shinobazu Pond is in the park, covers about 16 hectares and has wide lotus beds and a small island shrine to Benzaiten. Wintering birds gather there too. The five-story pagoda dates from 1639 and is one of the surviving temple buildings in the park. The National Museum of Western Art is a Le Corbusier building and is on the UNESCO World Heritage List.

For photos, think in layers: a tree-lined path in the foreground, blossom or leaves overhead, and the pond or a building behind. The park is large, so pick two or three spots and give each a few minutes rather than trying to cover it all. Wear comfortable shoes and keep your phone handy for quick shots as you walk. If you plan to go inside a museum or temple area, check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Ueno Park is in the Ueno district of Taitō, Tokyo, on Ueno Hill.
text.directions_text: The nearest station is Ueno, served by the JR Joban Line, JR Keihin-Tohoku-Negishi Line, JR Takasaki Line, JR Ueno-Tokyo Line, JR Utsunomiya Line, JR Yamanote Line, Tokyo Metro Ginza Line and Tokyo Metro Hibiya Line. The park is to the west of the station, about 8 minutes on foot. From Ueno-okachimachi, on the Toei Oedo Line, the park is to the north, also about 8 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 460 m north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for paths, trees and the pond as you see them. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for a whole avenue of trees or a wide pond view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for blossom branches, lotus leaves or birds on the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 460 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place a path along one of the lower lines so it leads the eye into the picture. Let overhanging branches fill the top corner as a natural frame. For the pond, keep the horizon level and include some foreground water or leaves. In busy areas, wait a few seconds for a gap in the crowd.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on your main subject to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky or pale blossom looks washed out. For blossom close-ups, tap on the flowers and keep the phone steady. Use portrait mode only if people or a single branch are close to you.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late March to early April is the usual time for cherry blossom, though the dates change from year to year. Outside blossom season, early morning is quieter and the light is softer, and late afternoon is warm and gentle. Summer is the time for lotus leaves and flowers on the pond.

text.access_note: The park itself is an open public space, but museums, the temple and shrine areas and some attractions inside it may be ticketed or have set hours, so check the official site before you go.

text.description: Kabukichō is Shinjuku's neon entertainment district, known for its signs and nightlife. Two things draw the camera. One is the red Kabuki-chō Ichiban-gai gate near the south-west corner on Yasukuni-Dōri, often photographed as the main entrance. The other is the Godzilla head, a life-size replica of the creature from the neck up, added in 2015 to an outdoor terrace of the Toho Shinjuku Building. The building stands where the old Shinjuku Koma Theatre used to be, and the head has become a local landmark. The name Kabukichō comes from late-1940s plans for a kabuki theatre. The theatre was never built, but the name stayed. The district covers about 36 hectares and is packed with bars, restaurants, cinemas and hotels. That density gives you layers of signs, lanterns and crowds in a single frame. It is also an area where some businesses add heavy hidden charges, so enjoy it from the street, do not follow anyone who invites you into a venue, and check bills carefully if you do go in. Take your photos from the pavement and keep the frame moving. Shoot signs and rooflines rather than close-ups of strangers, and step out of the flow of people when you stop to frame a shot. Give yourself time for a short loop: the gate first, then continue into the district to find the Toho Shinjuku Building and the Godzilla head.
text.geographic_location: Kabukichō is in Shinjuku, Tokyo. Yasukuni-Dōri runs along its southern edge, and the Shinjuku City Office is also in the district. The nearest stations are Higashi-shinjuku to the north-east of the district's centre and Shinjuku-sanchome to the south of it, each roughly 450 m away.

Once there, head for the phone icon on the map and then continue into the district to find the Toho Shinjuku Building and the Godzilla terrace. The phone icon on the map is about 350 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

Use the default lens (1x) for general street scenes. Use telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the Godzilla head from a distance and for picking out signs above the crowd.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: In the evening, tap on a bright sign to set focus, then slide the exposure slider down a little so the neon keeps its colour instead of turning white. If the phone offers night mode, hold still for the second or two it takes. Avoid shooting people close up.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Dusk and early evening, when the signs are lit but the sky still has some blue in it, tend to work best. Daytime is quieter and fine for the Godzilla head and the gate.

text.description:
Takeshita Street is a short, busy lane of small shops, snack stalls and cafés in the heart of Harajuku, the Shibuya district known around the world for Japanese youth culture and street fashion. It photographs well because everything is packed close together: colourful shopfronts, bold signs and a constant stream of people in all kinds of outfits. It is lively rather than pretty, and that energy is the picture.

A few facts help you read the scene. Before 1965 the area around the street was known locally as Takeshita-cho. In the 1980s the street became famous for teenage street-dancing groups called takenoko-zoku. Since the 1990s, international fashion chains have also moved into Harajuku, which sits alongside the independent boutiques.

For phone photos, think in layers. Take one wide shot of the whole crowded lane, then a few closer pictures of details such as a shop sign, a crepe in someone's hand or a bright window display. Keep your phone at chest height for a natural, street-level view, and take your time: the best frames come when you pause at the edge of the flow and let people walk through the scene. Be polite about photographing strangers up close, and ask before you shoot inside shops.

shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 280 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. Walk about 5 minutes on foot, then stand at the edge of the lane, out of the main flow of people, and shoot along it.

Try one shot with the crowd filling the frame and another with a clear foreground detail, such as a sign or a colourful treat. Keep the phone level so the buildings stay straight.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a face or a bright sign to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the colours stay rich and the bright signs don't wash out. A Live Photo can catch a good moment as people walk past. Use portrait mode only if you have someone's permission.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day it is usually calmer, which gives you clearer frames of the street and its shopfronts. Later in the day and at weekends it fills with people, which is good for energy but harder for clean compositions.

text.description: The Rainbow Bridge is the white suspension bridge that links the Shibaura waterfront on the Tokyo side with Odaiba across the northern part of Tokyo Bay. Its official name is the Tokyo Port Bridge, but the public chose "Rainbow Bridge" for the English name. It was built between 1987 and 1993 and is 798 m long, with a main span of 580 m. It works well in photos because the shape is simple and clean. Two white towers and sweeping cables stand against open water and sky. The towers are painted white to blend with central Tokyo as seen from Odaiba. After dark, lamps on the cables glow red, white and green, powered by solar energy collected during the day. That gives you a colourful subject for an evening picture without any extra effort. The bridge has two decks. The upper one carries an expressway, and the lower one carries a rail line, a road and a walkway on each outer side. The north walkway looks over the inner harbour towards Tokyo Tower, and the south walkway looks over the bay, and on clear days towards Mount Fuji. Wipe your phone lens first, because sea air and fingerprints soften the picture and cause glare around the lights.

The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the line of the deck along the lower third, leaving the towers and sky above. Keep the phone level so the deck stays straight. Include a little water in the foreground to give the picture depth.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bridge to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour. After dark, switch on night mode and rest your elbows on a rail or wall to keep the picture sharp. Wait for any passing people before pressing the shutter.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into dusk. You get soft light on the towers, then the cable lamps in red, white and green once it is dark.

text.description:
Shinjuku Gyoen is a large public garden in the middle of Tokyo, and it makes a calm change from the surrounding streets. It began as the residence of the Naitō family in the Edo period, and the family finished a garden here in 1772. The present layout opened in May 1906, after a remodel by the French-trained landscape architect Henry Martinet. The garden covers 58.3 hectares and blends three styles: French formal and English landscape in the north, and a traditional Japanese garden in the south. A traditional tea house stands in the grounds.

It photographs well because there is so much variety. You get open lawns, long lines of trees and, in spring, around 1,500 cherry trees that bloom from late March to late April. Tall Himalayan cedars rise above the rest of the garden. Look for them as a backdrop, or use a plane tree or cedar trunk to frame the foreground. Cherry blossom season is very popular, so expect crowds, and take your shots between the people rather than waiting for a clear view.

Start your photos there and then wander in. Entry rules, closing days and reservations change through the year, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Shinjuku Gyoen sits in central Tokyo, across the Shinjuku and Shibuya areas, close to Shinjuku-gyoemmae and Sendagaya stations. It is a large green block between busy city districts.
text.directions_text: The simplest route is from Shinjuku-gyoemmae (Tokyo Metro Marunouchi Line). The garden lies to the south of the station, about 403 m away (about 7 minutes on foot). You can also use Sendagaya (JR Chuo-Sobu Line), about 433 m away with the garden to the north (about 7 minutes on foot). Once you are near the garden, follow the signs and the flow of other visitors to the nearest gate. The phone icon on the map is about 90 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for general views of lawns and tree lines. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) when you want a whole row of trees or a blossom canopy in one frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as a single branch of blossom, a cedar top or the tea house roof.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 90 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. Take a few frames here, then walk in and repeat the same ideas from inside.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the upper or lower third line. Use a nearby branch or tree trunk at the edge of the frame to add depth. With ultra-wide, keep people and bright sky away from the corners, because they can look stretched there.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the main subject to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky looks washed out. For close blossom shots, try portrait mode to soften the background, or use the telephoto lens instead if portrait mode blurs the petals oddly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: The sources say the cherry trees bloom from late March to late April, with different varieties flowering at different times. Try to arrive early in the day for softer light and fewer people.

text.access_note: This is a national garden with set gates, closing days and, at cherry blossom time, reservations for some dates, so check the official site before you go.

text.description: Ginza is Tokyo's polished shopping district, and it photographs well because of its wide streets, tall shop fronts, glowing signs and the steady flow of people. The name comes from a silver-coin mint set up here in 1612. After a big fire in 1872 the area was rebuilt as a showpiece of modern, Western-style planning, and it has stayed fashionable ever since. Most of those early brick buildings are gone. One famous survivor is the Wakō building with its clock tower, which dates from 1894 and is the best-known landmark to look for. On Saturdays and Sundays from 12:00 to 17:00 the main street, Chūō-dōri, is closed to traffic. You can then stand in the road and shoot along it without cars, and street performers sometimes add life to the scene. Use the phone icon on the map as your starting spot, then walk towards the subject to find the best views of the shop fronts and the clock tower. On your phone, keep people and signs in the frame together to give a sense of scale, and wait a moment for gaps in the crowd. Shops may have their own rules about photographing inside, so keep your pictures to the street.

text.description: The Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building, known as the Tochō, is the seat of the Tokyo city government, and its two observation decks give you a high, wide view over Shinjuku and the city beyond. The decks sit on floor 45, about 202 metres up, with one in each tower. Both are free to the public and have cafes and gift shops. They are open from 9:30 to 22:00 on alternating days, so only one deck is open on any given day. The building was designed by Kenzo Tange and finished in December 1990. The twin-tower tower block is meant to resemble an integrated circuit while also recalling a Gothic cathedral, which makes it interesting from outside as well as from the top. For photographs, the appeal is the sheer scale of the skyline spreading out in every direction, and the chance to see the city change from daylight into evening lights if you stay on. Inside, you are shooting through large windows, so the main challenge is reflections rather than distance. Hold the phone close to the glass, shade it with your hand or jacket, and keep the screen brightness up so you can judge the shot. Outside, step back from the foot of the building to fit the twin towers into the frame. Check the official site before you go to confirm which deck is open that day.
text.geographic_location: In Shinjuku ward, Tokyo. The complex is right next to Tochomae station on the Toei Oedo Line, with Nishi-shinjuku station on the Tokyo Metro Marunouchi Line a little further away.
text.directions_text: The nearest station is Tochomae on the Toei Oedo Line, about 170 m away, which is about 3 minutes on foot; the building lies to the south-west of the station. You can also start from Nishi-shinjuku on the Tokyo Metro Marunouchi Line, about 563 m away, which is about 9 minutes on foot; the building lies to the south of that station. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for most skyline views from the deck. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the twin towers into the frame from outside, or to capture a wider sweep of the city from the window. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out distant towers or details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For outside shots, step back from the foot of the towers until the whole structure fits. For skyline views, stand at a window on the 45th-floor deck.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line up the horizon on the upper or lower third, depending on whether you want more sky or more city. From outside, tilt the phone up only slightly, so the tall towers do not lean inwards, and use the ultra-wide (0.5x) sparingly because it stretches the edges. text.description:
Yoyogi Park is a large, landscaped park in Shibuya, right beside Harajuku Station and Meiji Shrine. It photographs well because it is open and green, with plenty of space for wide scenes of lawns, trees and people enjoying themselves. On Sundays it becomes a gathering place for music fans, jugglers, martial arts clubs, cosplayers and other hobby groups, so there is often something lively to capture. In spring, crowds come for the cherry blossom, and the pink branches make a soft frame for a phone shot.

The park also has some history. It is the site of Japan's first successful powered aircraft flight, flown by Captain Yoshitoshi Tokugawa on 19 December 1910. The area was also used for the 1964 Summer Olympics, housing the main Olympic Village and the Yoyogi National Gymnasium, designed by Kenzo Tange. Both facts are good for a caption alongside your photo.

For practical photography, walk a little way in rather than shooting from the edge, as the best views open up once you are among the trees and lawns. Look for paths and avenues that lead the eye into the distance. If you photograph performers or groups, keep a respectful distance and ask before taking close portraits. Use the phone icon on the map as a starting place, then wander north through the park.
text.geographic_location: Yoyogi Park is in Shibuya, Tokyo, next to Harajuku Station and Meiji Shrine.
text.directions_text: The quickest way is to get off at Harajuku (JR Yamanote Line) and walk about 8 minutes on foot to the north-west to reach the park. Alternatively, use Meiji-jingumae 'Harajuku' (Tokyo Metro Chiyoda Line or Tokyo Metro Fukutoshin Line), about 12 minutes on foot to the north-west. The phone icon on the map is about 500 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for natural-looking views of paths, trees and people. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) for big lawn scenes or cherry blossom overhead. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out performers or details from a polite distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 500 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. From there, walk into the park to find the open views.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place a path or tree line on one of the lines so it leads into the picture. Keep some foreground, such as grass or blossom branches, to give a sense of depth. With ultra-wide, keep people away from the edges of the frame, where they can look stretched.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on your subject to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if bright sky is washing out the scene. In spring, try portrait mode for a person in front of blossom. Live Photos can capture movement from street performers and dancers.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunday is the liveliest day for people-watching, and spring is the season for cherry blossom. Earlier in the day tends to be quieter, with softer light.

text.access_note: Yoyogi Park is a public park, but check the official site before you go in case of closures or event restrictions.

text.description:
The Imperial Palace is the main residence of the emperor of Japan. It sits in a large, park-like area in Chiyoda, Tokyo, on the site of the old Edo Castle. The grounds cover about 1.15 square kilometres. Nijūbashi refers to the double bridges over the moat. The original wooden double bridges over the moat were replaced with stone and iron ones in the Meiji period. It photographs well because you get a wide stretch of moat, old stone walls and greenery, with the city's office towers behind. That mix of old and new makes a good phone picture.

Most of the palace grounds are generally closed to the public. Reserved guided tours run from Tuesday to Saturday, and the public may also enter on 2 January and 23 February. The East Gardens, the former inner compounds of Edo Castle, are a public park, and the park to the north is also open. So most visitors take their photos from outside, across the moat. Plan on a wide scene with the water and walls in front, or use zoom to pick out the bridge and rooflines. Keep a little of the moat or wall in the foreground so the picture has depth. Check the official site before you go if you want to join a tour or enter the gardens.
text.geographic_location: In the Chiyoda district of Chiyoda ward, in central Tokyo, on the former Edo Castle site. The East Gardens and Kitanomaru Park lie around it, and Kokyo Gaien National Garden is to the south.
text.directions_text: The nearest station is Sakuradamon (Tokyo Metro Yūrakuchō Line), about 9 minutes on foot, with the palace area to the north. Alternatively, take Nijubashimae 'Marunouchi' (Tokyo Metro Chiyoda Line), about 14 minutes on foot, with the palace to the west. Once nearby, walk to the phone icon on the map and look north-west. The phone icon on the map is about 350 m south-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole scene of moat, wall and sky. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want to include more foreground water or stonework. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the bridge and palace rooflines from a distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 350 m south-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the moat or stone wall along the lower third. Leave the trees and any rooftops in the upper part. At 2x or more, frame the bridge or a roofline with a little water or greenery around it. Hold the phone with both hands, as zoomed shots show every wobble.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework or trees to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright, so the sky keeps its colour. Try a Live Photo to catch a moving boat or passing walkers, but take a normal shot as well.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows on the walls than midday. Check the weather first, as a clear day makes the water and sky look good.

text.description:
Omoide Yokocho is a tight group of small lanes in Nishi-Shinjuku, right beside Shinjuku station. It is a good place for atmospheric street photos, because everything is close together and the scene is full of texture. Expect signs, lanterns, steam and the glow of small shopfronts packed side by side. On a phone, those crowded details make a lively, layered picture without any special skill.

Start there for a wide establishing shot. Then walk closer and take smaller pictures of doorways, signs and lights. The lanes are narrow, so a wide view is hard to get from inside them. The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) helps you fit in more of the scene.

It is a lively area, so keep an eye on people walking past and stay out of doorways. If a close-up includes a customer or a member of staff, ask first. Wipe your lens before you start, because street haze and cooking steam can make night shots look soft.

The nearest station, Shinjuku-nishiguchi on the Toei Oedo Line, is only a short walk away, so this is an easy place to fit in between other Shinjuku stops.
text.geographic_location: Omoide Yokocho is in Nishi-Shinjuku 1-chome, in Shinjuku ward, Tokyo, on the west side of Shinjuku station and about 29 m east of Shinjuku-nishiguchi station on the Toei Oedo Line.
text.directions_text: The nearest station is Shinjuku-nishiguchi (Toei Oedo Line), about 1 minute on foot, with the spot to the east of the station. Shinjuku (JR Chuo JC Section Line, JR Chuo Line, JR Chuo Rapid Line, JR Chuo-Sobu Line, JR Saikyo Line, JR Shonan-Shinjuku Line, JR Yamanote Line, Toei Oedo Line and Tokyo Metro Marunouchi Line) is also close, about 7 minutes on foot, with the spot to the north of the station. The phone icon on the map is about 45 m north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 45 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south. Stay out of the way of people walking past.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the verticals straight. Use the lane's lines to lead the eye in, and place the brightest lights or signs on a third of the frame. For a second shot, move closer and frame a single doorway or sign.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a bright sign to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the lights keep their colour and do not turn white. In the evening, turn on night mode and hold the phone against your body or a wall to stay steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early evening, when the lights come on but there is still some colour in the sky, usually works well. Daytime gives a clearer view of the buildings but a flatter mood.

text.description:
The Hachikō statue stands in Hachiko Square, right beside Shibuya station. The photo can be as much about the people and the city around it as about the statue. That is why it works well on a phone: you can show the statue small and let the crowds, signs and buildings tell you where you are.

The phone icon on the map is about 40 m north-west of the subject. From there the statue is small in the frame. Use it for a scene-setting shot, then walk closer for a tighter picture. The square is often busy, so be patient. Wait a few moments and a gap usually opens up around the statue. Keep to the edge of the walkways so you do not block people heading to the station.

The statue is only about 2 minutes on foot from the station, so it is easy to combine with other stops nearby. Take a wide shot first, then a closer one, and you will have two very different photos in a couple of minutes.
text.geographic_location: In Shibuya, in Tokyo's Shibuya ward, at Hachiko Square, about 120 m to the west of Shibuya station.
text.directions_text: Head for Shibuya station, served by the JR Saikyo Line, JR Shonan-Shinjuku Line, JR Yamanote Line, Tokyo Metro - Denentoshi bypass line, Tokyo Metro Fukutoshin Line, Tokyo Metro Ginza Line and Tokyo Metro Hanzōmon Line. The statue is about 123 m to the west of the station, about 2 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 40 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) at the phone icon on the map to show the statue in its square. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a closer view without stepping into the crowd. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are standing close and want the buildings behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 40 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. For a closer shot, walk towards the statue along the edge of the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the statue on one of the lower thirds, with the square and buildings filling the rest. Wait for a moment when fewer people stand directly in front of it. For a close shot, hold the phone low and level so the statue does not look tilted.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the statue to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky behind is bright. In a crowd, a Live Photo lets you pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is usually quieter, and the evening gives lit signs and a livelier mood. Use night mode after dark and hold the phone steady.

text.access_note: The statue is in an open public square beside the station, but check the official site before you go in case of any works or changes.
